transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Whenever we’re supposed to sit and do quiet activities here at my senior living complex, I just can’t seem to keep myself still and focused on them. It has been quite frustrating since I moved in, as there are so many expectations for us to just sit quietly.
Have you always had trouble sitting still, even when you were younger, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, it’s actually a lifelong thing. Even back in grade school, my teachers were constantly telling me to stay in my seat and stop blurting out answers, and my mother always said I was "on the go" from the moment I woke up. It has just become much more of a problem since I moved into this senior complex about a year and a half ago because of all the structured, quiet activities they expect us to sit through.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F90.0", "F41.1", "F32.0"], but based on this conversation, both F41.1 and F32.0 seem unlikely because there are no reported symptoms of generalized anxiety or depressive episodes such as low mood, excessive worry, or anhedonia. Instead, the patient describes a lifelong pattern of difficulty with stillness, restlessness, and impulsivity dating back to childhood, which strongly supports F90.0. The persistence of symptoms into older age and the lifelong history make F90.0 the only plausible candidate.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong history of symptoms consistent with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type, with onset in childhood and persistent difficulties in remaining still and controlling impulsive behaviors. Symptoms are now causing functional impairment in the current setting due to increased environmental demands for sedentary behavior.
